result.markdown: --- title: "Nonuniform grids" engine: julia --- On a uniform grid every kernel copy is the same polynomial, shifted. On a nonuniform grid the spacing changes from interval to interval, and the Julia package carries a second family of kernels whose polynomial pieces are recomputed for the actual knots, so that the interpolant keeps its cardinality and its polynomial reproduction on any strictly increasing knot vector. Nothing needs to be switched on: passing knots that are not uniformly spaced selects them. The Python port works on uniform grids only, so far; the [feature matrix](../features.qmd) tracks the port. ## The kernels Two kinds of nonuniform kernel are available: - `:n3` is the nonuniform cubic, the counterpart of `:a3`: closed-form weights, a four-wide stencil and no precomputation, so it costs about what the uniform cubic costs. It is the default on nonuniform grids. - `:b5` to `:b13` are the nonuniform counterparts of the high-order kernels. They converge at order degree + 1 — `:b5` at 6th order and `:b13` at 14th — and provide derivatives up to 7th order. Their weights are projected onto each interval in exact rational arithmetic when the interpolant is built, so construction costs one projection per interval and grows with the number of intervals; evaluation is as local as on a uniform grid. The uniform `:a` kernels other than `:a3` have no nonuniform counterpart. ## A first example A damped sine sampled on a grid that is dense where the function varies fast and sparse where it has settled, interpolated with `:b7` and differentiated twice: ::: {#4 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} x = [0.0, 0.15, 0.4, 0.7, 1.5, 2.5, 3.8, 4.2, 4.6, 4.8, 5.0, 5.3, 5.6, 6.0, 6.5, 7.0, 7.3, 7.8, 8.2, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0] # an irregular knot vector f(x) = sin(x) * exp(-x / 5) # the function being sampled y = f.(x) # the values at the knots itp = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7) # nonuniform grid detected from the knots d1 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7, derivative = 1) # its first derivative d2 = convolution_interpolation(x, y; kernel = :b7, derivative = 2) # its second derivative xf = range(0, 10, length = 600) # fine points for plotting fig = Figure(size = (800, 400)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "x") lines!(ax, xf, itp.(xf); label = "interpolant") lines!(ax, xf, d1.(xf); label = "first derivative") lines!(ax, xf, d2.(xf); label = "second derivative") lines!(ax, xf, f.(xf); color = :black, label = "f") scatter!(ax, x, y; markersize = 10, color = :white, strokecolor = :black, strokewidth = 1.5, label = "knots") Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | at x = 2.9 (a sparse part of the grid) | f | f′ | |:--|--:|--:| | interpolant | 0.1340734324 | -0.5704459029 | | exact | 0.1339553086 | -0.5704289524 | ## Convergence on a graded grid The orders hold on nonuniform grids as they do on uniform ones. Here the knots are a uniform grid pushed through a smooth monotone map, so that each refinement keeps the grading and halves every spacing, and Runge's function is interpolated with four kernels: ::: {#8 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="The convergence study"} runge(x) = 1 / (1 + 25x^2) # Runge's function grade(u) = u + 0.3 * sin(π * u) / π # a monotone map of [−1, 1] onto itself, dense near the centre xr = range(-1, 1, length = 2001) # fine points for measuring the error kernels = (:n3, :b5, :b7, :b9, :b11) ns = [41, 81, 161, 321, 641] # the numbers of knots hs = 2 ./ (ns .- 1) # the spacings of the uniform grid before grading errors = [begin xn = grade.(range(-1, 1, length = n)) # the graded knots itp_k = convolution_interpolation(xn, runge.(xn); kernel = k) maximum(abs.(itp_k.(xr) .- runge.(xr))) end for n in ns, k in kernels] fig = Figure(size = (800, 420)) ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xscale = log10, yscale = log10, xreversed = true, xlabel = "mean spacing h", ylabel = "largest error") for (j, k) in enumerate(kernels) scatterlines!(ax, hs, max.(errors[:, j], 1e-17); markersize = 8, label = string(k)) end Legend(fig[1, 2], ax) fig ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: | | `n3` | `b5` | `b7` | `b9` | `b11` | |:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:| | observed convergence order | 3.00 | 5.84 | 7.72 | 9.14 | 11.01 | ## In more dimensions Nonuniform knots can be given per axis, and the grid is the tensor product of the axes, so a log-spaced axis and a uniform axis combine freely. Each axis chooses its own kernel and derivative order: ::: {#12 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.julia .cell-code} xg = 10 .^ range(-2, 0, length = 25) # a log-spaced axis on [0.01, 1] yg = range(0, 1, length = 20) # a uniform axis data = [log(xi) * cos(π * yi) for xi in xg, yi in yg] # log(x)·cos(πy) on the grid itp2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; kernel = :b7) # interpolation dx2 = convolution_interpolation((xg, yg), data; kernel = (:b7, :b5), derivative = (1, 0)) # ∂/∂x, two kernels itp2(0.05, 0.3), dx2(0.05, 0.3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (-1.7608755746816087, 11.746837334411147) ``` ::: ::: | at (0.05, 0.3) | f | ∂f/∂x | |:--|--:|--:| | interpolant | -1.7608755747 | 11.7468373344 | | exact | -1.7608472502 | 11.7557050458 | The precomputation of the `:b` kernels is per interval and per axis, so it stays cheap on a tensor-product grid: a 1000 × 1000 grid needs two thousand projections, not a million. ## What is not available Antiderivatives are uniform-grid only: the precomputed tails that make an integral cost the same as an interpolation rely on equal spacing. To integrate data on a nonuniform grid, evaluate the nonuniform interpolant on a uniform grid fine enough to carry it and integrate that with `derivative = -1`, as on the [integrals page](integrals.qmd). Lazy construction, for large grids, is available with `:n3` only; the `:b` kernels build their ghost values when the interpolant is created.
